Complete freedom? Free as long as it doesn't cause physical harm? Ban slander/libel? Ban hate speech?

What do you say?
What, if any, should be the limitations of free speech?

What's your conception of freedom? Doesn't it have requirements? If not, wouldn't 'complete freedom' be redundant? What is speech? And why it seems like speech limitation is represented by banishment?

I wouldn't say the concept of "complete freedom" is redundant for the way most people understand "free speech". Most people in the US believe they have freedom of speech but there are legal limitations to how they can use it. They aren't allowed to endanger others by starting a riot, calling in a bomb threat, or yelling "fire" in a crowded theater. Slander and libel have civil penalties. Public nudity and sex in most places is illegal. Even with those and myriad other exceptions, most US citizens would still claim they have freedom of speech.

Complete freedom would mean lifting all legal prohibitions against speech/art/expression/etc.

I'm aware of the common conception of freedom of speech, just wanted to make a little brain stretching. I don't think that endangering other is the sufficient criteria for limitation. If we understand the examples you cited, it's mostly based of tangible harm, and a sense of responsibility that leads to compensation. My position is that whenever someone, by his act or his fault, causes a material or a moral harm to others, with no legal authority, he has to offer a compensation. As for exercising one's right to free speech, the principle is that no one is liable of making use of his right with no willful misconduct, but when exercising such right is causing a notable harm to others, said harm being possibly avoided with no inconvenience to him, he is liable when he does nothing to prevent or stop said harm.
What do you mean by "moral harm to others"?
I'm with you on the slander, but insults are in the eye of the beholder. Public defamation may cause harm, but if what is being said is factually true the person saying it isn't liable for the harm.
Of course, the harm has to be proven, and the idea of defamation implies non factual allegations.
Without defining "freedom" and without defining "speech" it's impossible to have this conversation because people will conceptualize those to mean wildly different things.

Is that a problem? Both terms are by nature fairly fluid and subjective. Leaving them generalized allows a dialectic to happen.

If I gave a precise definition based on my views it would basically turn into a discussion about my definition.

Problem? No. Be it via dialectic, without defining the root words, we can't really have a discussion on what is free speech.

Is speech verbal or written dialogue? Am I speaking when I dance? Am I speaking when I give money to an American political campaign? The last two examples seem to directly contradict the very word. Did you mean expression?

Is freedom the ability to do as I please in every case, without constraint? Do you mean civic freedom, or an analog to degrees of motion? Those two ideas are very different.

A lot of people have been having this conversation for a long time, some of us don't want to literally start from a completely deconstructed "primordial" concept of "freedom" and "speech," it's exhausting. I understand you don't want to constrain the conversation, but leaving the terms maximally generalized is completely unproductive for anyone who's actually stopped to think about it before now.

Don't get me wrong, I'm not trying to discourage. I just want to see that at the very least the person I'm about to have a conversation with, in a topic that is actually extremely important and nontrivial in complexity, has actually put some thought into it.

I would think that most people that have put any thought into "free speech" know that the conversation usually includes "expression". As such, the post title "What, if any, should be the limitations of free speech" allows the participant to define "freedom" and "speech" as they wish. If they wish to limit "speech" to only being verbal that is their prerogative, but they will have to defend that limitation.

The same applies to "freedom". If they wish to take a maximalist position where there is no constraint, they should expect to defend it against concerns for public safety and slander/libel. If they want to take the position that a government has the power to limit free speech for the public good, they should be ready to defend themselves against more libertarian ideals.

Even if the discussion starts from an extremely generalized concept it is still one that is worth having. At worst, it fleshes out where the zeitgeist of voat stands. At best, a productive conversation will happen and some readers may be exposed to ideas they hadn't been exposed to before.
